title: Bhakti: the Upanishad's last word
hookLine: a sage finishes six chapters of hard teaching and ends on one word: love
carry: bhakti: the teaching shines for one who loves
tomorrow: what one line holds all the Upanishads?
last: THE ONE IN YOUR HEART IS GREATER THAN THE SKY — SMALL AND GREAT.

cards: On a festival night at a Hindu temple, the sound can reach the street before you reach the door: bells, drums, a crowd singing one name over and over, someone in tears at the front.
That whole world of love poured toward God has a name, bhakti, devotion. You met it in year one with Mirabai and the saints. But where does the word first show up in these old texts?
You have to read to the very end of the Shvetashvatara, to its final verse.

teach.h: TAPAS, AND THE GRACE OF GOD.
teach.b: The Shvetashvatara is named for its teacher, and near the end the text tells his story in a few lines.
By the power of his tapas, his discipline, and by the grace of God, the wise Shvetashvatara came to know Brahman, and he taught it to seekers who had left everything else behind.
Notice the order: his own effort, and then grace. He doesn't take the credit alone.

And then the very last verse, 6.23, in paraphrase: for the great soul who has the highest devotion to God, and the same devotion to the teacher as to God, these things that have been taught shine out.

Bhakti comes from a root, bhaj, to share, to take part, to belong. Scholars often point to this verse as the first time the word bhakti appears in the principal Upanishads in this sense, devotion to a personal God.
Six chapters of wheels, swans and fire sticks, and the last verse doesn't add more knowledge.

teach.h: IT SHINES FOR THE ONE WHO LOVES.
teach.b: It says the knowledge shines for the one who loves. That's the teaching Hindus live at every bhajan night and every aarti: God is known by love, not by thinking alone.
And the teacher is part of it, which is why a Hindu student bows to the guru, and a young dancer or musician touches the teacher's feet before a lesson.
Not everyone reads it alike: Advaita teachers often treat devotion as what readies the mind for knowledge, while devotional schools treat it as the goal itself.

how: Bhakti is lived across Hindu traditions through kirtan and bhajan singing, temple worship, repeating God's name, and honoring one's teacher, and many devotees treat love of God as the heart of practice.

o: devotion: love of God, a sense of belonging
a strict rule for worship in the temple
the knowledge that frees the soul at death

games.q: Shvetashvatara knew Brahman by his own tapas and by something more, and his last verse says what makes the teaching shine. what is it?
o: a sharper mind for the hard verses.
the grace of God, and the highest devotion to God and to the teacher.
games.why: tapas and the grace of God, says 6.21. and 6.23: the teaching shines for one with para bhakti, to God and to the guru as to God. the last word is love.

practice: Bhakti is practiced out loud, so try it softly. If you pray, choose one name of God that's yours, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, Devi, or simply om, and say or sing it slowly, again and again, for the sit.
If you don't pray, say the name of a teacher who gave you something, and let thanks come with it. Let the name do the work, the way one name carries a whole room at a bhajan night.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion, from a root that means to share or to belong. Its first appearance in the principal Upanishads is in the Shvetashvatara's last verse.

orig.note: Sanskrit bhakti: devotion, from bhaj, to share or belong. first used in this sense in the principal Upanishads at Shvetashvatara 6.23.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti, the teaching shines for one who loves. Tomorrow, one line to hold all seven Upanishads. See you then.
